etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English coveren, borrowed from Old French covrir, cueuvrir (modern French couvrir), from Late Latin coperire, from Latin cooperiō (“I cover completely”), from co- (intensive prefix) + operiō (“I close, cover”). Displaced native Middle English thecchen and bethecchen (“to cover”) (from Old English þeccan, beþeccan (“to cover”)), Middle English helen, (over)helen, (for)helen (“to cover, conceal”) (from Old English helan (“to conceal, cover, hide”)), Middle English wrien, (be)wreon (“to cover”) (from Old English (be)wrēon (“to cover”)), Middle English hodren, hothren (“to cover up”) (from Low German hudren (“to cover up”)).

According to the Oxford English Dictionary, the original sense of the verb and noun cover was “hide from view” as in its cognate covert. Except in the limited sense of “cover again”, the word recover is unrelated and is cognate with recuperate. Cognate with Spanish cubrir (“to cover”).

definitions.definition: A lid.
(uncountable) Area or situation which screens a person or thing from view.
The front and back of a book, magazine, CD package, etc.
The top sheet of a bed.
A cloth or similar material, often fitted, placed over an item such as a car or sofa or food to protect it from dust, rain, insects, etc. when not being used.
A cover charge.
A setting at a restaurant table or formal dinner.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter I, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: When I gave a dinner there was generally a cover laid for him. I liked the man for his own sake, and even had he promised to turn out a celebrity it would have had no weight with me.

definitions.definition: (music) A new performance or rerecording of a previously recorded song; a cover version; a cover song.
(cricket) A fielding position on the off side, between point and mid off, about 30° forward of square; a fielder in this position.
(cricket) A tarpaulin or other device used to cover the wicket during rain, to prevent it getting wet.
(combinatorics, topology) A collection (or family) of subsets of a given set, whose union contains every element of said original set.
(philately) An envelope complete with stamps and postmarks etc.
(military) A solid object, including terrain, that provides protection from enemy fire.

(law) In commercial law, a buyer’s purchase on the open market of goods similar or identical to the goods contracted for after a seller has breached a contract of sale by failure to deliver the goods contracted for.
(insurance) An insurance contract; coverage by an insurance contract.
(espionage) A persona maintained by a spy or undercover operative; cover story.
(dated) A swindler's confederate.
The portion of a slate, tile, or shingle that is hidden by the overlap of the course above.[1]
In a steam engine, the lap of a slide valve.
(construction) The distance between reinforcing steel and the exterior of concrete.
Of or pertaining to the front cover of a book or magazine.
(music) Of, pertaining to, or consisting of cover versions.
(transitive) To place something over or upon, as to conceal or protect.
(transitive) To be over or upon, as to conceal or protect.

quote.citation: 1913, Mrs. [Marie] Belloc Lowndes, chapter I, in The Lodger, London: Methuen, →OCLC; republished in Novels of Mystery: The Lodger; The Story of Ivy; What Really Happened, New York, N.Y.: Longmans, Green and Co., […], [1933], →OCLC, page 0016:
quote.text: A great bargain also had been the excellent Axminster carpet which covered the floor; as, again, the arm-chair in which Bunting now sat forward, staring into the dull, small fire.

quote.citation: 2013 May-June, Charles T. Ambrose, “Alzheimer’s Disease”, in American Scientist, volume 101, number 3, page 200:
quote.text: Similar studies of rats have employed four different intracranial resorbable, slow sustained release systems— […]. Such a slow-release device containing angiogenic factors could be placed on the pia mater covering the cerebral cortex and tested in persons with senile dementia in long term studies.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To be upon all of, so as to completely conceal.
(transitive) To set upon all of, so as to completely conceal.
(intransitive, dated) To put on one's hat.

quote.citation: 1904, Rawdon Lubbock Brown, Calendar of State Papers and Manuscripts:
quote.text: All the while he held his hat in his hand; and even until he had given his answer, when he covered and bade us be.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To invest (oneself with something); to bring upon (oneself).

quote.text: the powers that covered themselves with everlasting infamy by the partition of Poland

definitions.definition: (transitive, of a publication) To discuss thoroughly; to provide coverage of.
(transitive) To deal with or include someone or something.

quote.citation: 2010 (publication date), "Contributors", Discover, ISSN 0274-7529, volume 32, number 1, January–February 2011, page 7:
quote.text: Richard Morgan covers science for The Economist, The New York Times, Scientific American, and Wired.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To have as an assignment or responsibility.
(transitive) To provide insurance coverage for.
To have under one’s scope or purview.
(transitive) To be enough money for.
(transitive) To supply with funds; to settle or pay the costs for; to foot the bill for.
(intransitive) To act as a replacement.
(transitive, broadcasting) To air or run locally originated material in place of network material during an internal spot break in a syndicated program.
(music, transitive) To make a cover version of (a song that was originally recorded by another artist).
(transitive) To protect from attack in general, to guard.

quote.citation: 1712 (date written), [Joseph] Addison, Cato, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  J[acob] Tonson, […], published 1713, →OCLC, Act I, scene i, page 2:
quote.text: Pent up in Utica he vainly formsA poor Epitome of Roman Greatneſs,And, cover’d with Numidian Guards, directsA feeble Army, and an empty Senate,Remnants of mighty Battels fought in vain.

definitions.definition: (military, law enforcement, transitive) To protect using an aimed firearm and the threat of firing; or to protect using continuous, heaving fire at or in the direction of the enemy so as to force the enemy to remain in cover; or to threaten using an aimed firearm.
(chess, transitive) To protect or control (a piece or square).
(sports, transitive) To defend (mark) a particular player or area.
(transitive) To provide an alibi for (someone); to provide excuses or apologia for (someone); to carry water for someone.
To protect, to guard.
(transitive) To copulate with (said of certain male animals such as dogs and horses).

quote.citation: 1927, Havelock Ellis, Studies in the Psychology of Sex, Volume 2 (of 6)‎[1]:
quote.text: Among animals in a domesticated or confined state it is easy to find evidence of homosexual attraction, due merely to the absence of the other sex. This was known to the ancients; the Egyptians regarded two male partridges as the symbol of homosexuality, and Aristotle noted that two female pigeons would cover each other if no male was at hand.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To extend over a given period of time or range, to occupy, to stretch over a given area.
(transitive) To traverse or put behind a certain distance.

quote.text: November 22 — Owing to bad weather all machines flew at a height of 5,000 feet and covered the 90 miles in just 90 minutes . November 23 — During fourth lap ...

quote.citation: 1989, Robert K. Krick, Parker's Virginia Battery, C.S.A.:
quote.text: It had covered better than 840 miles in just a few hours more than seven days.32 The apparently clumsily managed shuffle through the various railroad nets ...

definitions.definition: (transitive, dated) To arrange plates, etc. on (a table) in preparation for a meal.

quote.citation: 1892, George Chase, Leading Cases Upon the Law of Torts, page 46:
quote.text: […]  he told plaintiff he would cover the table, and furnish it the same as the one he was sitting at, and that he should be waited upon and served the same as those on the other side of the room.
